performers: Kerstin Thorborg, contralto; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Carl Martin Öhmann sings the tenor songs of the same concert)
intro: Muted violins move softly beneath a solitary oboe, and Kerstin Thorborg sings of frost, a cold wind and a lamp that has gone out. The second song of Das Lied von der Erde saves its great outburst for a plea to the sun of love.

sections.label: A · Frost beside the lake
sections.mNote: A solo oboe sings above muted violin quavers

sections.label: B · A cold wind bends the flowers
sections.mNote: Clarinet trills shiver around the alto’s line

sections.label: C · The strings sing without the voice
sections.mNote: Violins and violas press forward in a long crescendo

sections.label: A′ · A weary heart, an extinguished lamp
sections.mNote: The moving quavers return beneath the alto’s restrained voice

sections.label: D · The sun of love
sections.mNote: Two harps sweep beneath the alto’s E♭-major plea

sections.label: Coda · A question, then the oboe
sections.mNote: The voice falls silent; woodwinds finish the song

cues.title: The oboe above the frost
cues.text: Muted first violins set out in quiet, unbroken quavers. A solo oboe begins a long melody above them. Mahler marks the music weary and somewhat creeping; the little violin steps continue even when the oboe pauses for breath.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition full score, p. 39: Etwas schleichend. Ermüdet, muted first violins and oboe marked molto espressivo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A woman at her loom
cues.text: Behind the song stands a poem by Qian Qi: a woman weaves through a long autumn night beside a failing lamp. Judith Gautier’s French adaptation drops the loom. Through Hans Bethge’s German version, the frost, fading light and loneliness reach Mahler.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives prints Qian Qi’s Imitation of Old Poem: Long Autumn Night beside Gautier, Bethge and Mahler’s versions, identifying Gautier’s omissions. http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Einsame.htm

cues.title: Blue mist on the lake
cues.text: The flute echoes the oboe. The alto begins quietly in D minor: autumn mist drifts blue over a lake, and frost lies on the grass like jade dust scattered by an artist. The moving violin line continues beneath the scene.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 39–41: flute Echo and opening vocal stanza. Mahler Archives supplies the German text and its earlier versions.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler needs his walks
cues.text: In July 1908, while composing these songs, Mahler struggles with his doctors’ restrictions on exercise. He writes to Bruno Walter: “I can’t work at a desk. For my inner activity I need outer activity.”
cues.evidence: Mahler to Bruno Walter, 18 July 1908, quoted by Stephen E. Hefling in his Universal Edition introduction, March 2010. https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: The strings take the words
cues.text: After the golden lotus petals drift across the water, the singer falls silent. Violins and violas press into a tender, passionate melody. Winds and horns swell with them, then the music sinks back through the cellos.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 43–44, figure 10: Zart drängend, zart leidenschaftlich in violins and violas, wind and horn crescendo, then cello diminuendo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The little lamp goes out
cues.text: The opening pace returns with “Mein Herz ist müde” — my heart is weary. The alto sings without expression as the quavers pass through violas and cellos. Then the little lamp goes out with a crackle, and the strings play close to the bridge.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 44, figure 11: Tempo I, alto p ohne Ausdruck, viola and cello quavers, and am Steg in the violas under the lamp’s extinguishing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A place to rest
cues.text: The singer turns towards a familiar resting place and asks for peace. Mahler marks the voice heartfelt. A solo violin answers, while the flowing accompaniment carries on beneath the plea.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 45, figure 13: Ich komm zu dir, traute Ruhestätte, alto innig, solo violin and continuing string quavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sun of love
cues.text: Two harps sweep together beneath the singer’s great plea in E♭ major: will the sun of love never shine again? The voice stretches the word for love across the bar, then presses on towards the bitter tears.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 47–49, figure 18: Mit großem Aufschwung, E♭-major harmony, harps in unison and sustained Liebe.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One word makes it gentler
cues.text: The full orchestra falls away. Over plucked cellos, the alto asks whether those tears will ever be dried gently. Mahler adds that last kindness — “mild” — to Bethge’s poem, then gives the remaining music to the instruments.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 49, figure 19: Tempo I subito, p ohne Ausdruck and pizzicato cellos. Mahler Archives shows that mild is absent from Bethge’s text.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violin steps grow faint
cues.text: Oboe, bassoon and horn finish their phrases over the first violins’ continuing quavers. The violins slow and hold their last note. A few wind notes remain, marked to die away.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 50: woodwind and horn phrases over first violins, final Rit., pianississimo violins and morendo wind chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Clarinet trills bring the cold wind
transitions.to: B · A cold wind bends the flowers
transitions.how: The oboe’s phrase subsides and the moving first violins fall silent. Over soft winds, the alto begins the second stanza, about flowers whose scent has gone. The voice is marked very restrained; then clarinet trills shiver beneath the words about the cold wind.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 42, figures 7–8: first-violin rests, pp sehr gehalten in the voice and clarinet trills beneath ein kalter Wind.

transitions.title: The solo cello joins the section
transitions.from: B · A cold wind bends the flowers
transitions.to: C · The strings sing without the voice
transitions.how: A solo cello answers the alto’s words about lotus petals on the water. At Zart drängend, the singer stops and the full cello section joins the violins and violas. Their rising phrases draw in woodwinds and horns, all pressing towards a crescendo.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 43, figures 9–10: solo cello, Tutti and Zart drängend.

transitions.title: The cellos dwindle to four p’s
transitions.from: C · The strings sing without the voice
transitions.to: A′ · A weary heart, an extinguished lamp
transitions.how: The wind and string crescendo ends at fortissimo. The violins soften, and repeated cello quavers dwindle to pianississimo and beyond. Tempo I restores the opening pace; violas carry the moving notes beneath the alto’s plain statement that the heart is weary.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 44: Wieder zurückhaltend, cello diminuendo to pppp, then figure 11, Tempo I.

transitions.title: Two harps carry the plea
transitions.from: A′ · A weary heart, an extinguished lamp
transitions.how: The singer’s long autumn grows into an orchestral crescendo. Two harps enter with sweeping unison arpeggios. In E♭ major, at Mit großem Aufschwung, the alto reaches for the sun of love; the winds soften beneath the beginning of this long phrase.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 47–48, figure 18: harps in unison, E♭ major, Mit großem Aufschwung and pianissimo winds.

transitions.title: A quiet question over plucked cellos
transitions.to: Coda · A question, then the oboe
transitions.how: The harps keep sweeping as the alto presses through the words about bitter tears. Then the first tempo returns abruptly, with nearly every instrument silent. The singer finishes the question over plucked cellos. Bassoon and oboe begin the postlude.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 49–50, figure 19: Drängend, Tempo I subito and the transition to the postlude.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, II. Der Einsame im Herbst, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 39–50: oboe and muted violins at the opening; string interlude at figure 10; Tempo I at figure 11; harp arpeggios at figures 17–19; woodwind postlude on p. 50.

timeline.note: Muted first violins begin; the solo oboe enters above their quavers.
Clarinets and horns join the oboe as both violin sections move in quavers.
Violas and cellos enter; the flute echoes the oboe.
The alto’s first stanza unfolds above quiet winds and strings.
A long horn phrase accompanies the alto’s description of the frost.
Stopped horns, bassoons and bass clarinet sound a low chord beneath the voice.
The second stanza begins quietly over held woodwinds.
Clarinet trills shiver beneath the alto’s words about the cold wind.
A solo cello answers the singer’s tender phrases about the golden leaves.
The singer rests while strings, woodwinds and horns make a long crescendo.
Fortissimo wind and string chords subside into the cellos’ repeated quavers.
Violas resume the moving quavers beneath the alto’s weary heart.
A solo violin answers the plea for rest, above muted horns and moving strings.
Flute and alto sing above the first violins’ running semiquavers.
Two harps sweep in unison as the singer reaches towards the sun of love.
The first tempo returns; plucked cellos accompany the alto’s final question.
Bassoon, oboe and horn finish their phrases over the violin quavers.
The violin quavers slow to a held note beneath the last wind chords.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Kerstin Thorborg (contralto), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Named in the item title (“Concertgebouw Amsterdam”) and in the Mahler Foundation’s listing of a live Amsterdam concert; “Concertgebouw” names both the orchestra and the hall, and neither source names a room.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The item names no label and does not state the medium it was copied from. The Mahler Foundation’s discography records a Bel Age CD made “from acetates” of the broadcast; whether this file derives from that issue is not stated.

fields.label: Catalogue

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides

fields.label: Transfer date

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Internet Archive derivatives of a WAV original: this file is a variable-bit-rate MP3 (169 kbps); FLAC and spectrogram derivatives of the same WAV are also listed.
fields.note: The item description calls it “a good recording”. It does not describe noise reduction, speed correction or equalisation.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
